text: Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success on images to the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane, neither of which exists on curved surfaces. Developing deep learning techniques for geometric data is an active and fruitful research area. A common workaround maps a surface to a planar domain and applies a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either introduce large area distortion or require several images to cover the whole shape. We propose a new representation for sphere-type surfaces based on general covering maps. Rather than relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction lets a flat torus wrap around the surface several times, so that every region appears with low distortion somewhere in a single image. Because this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. This paper tackles the problem of sphere-type surface learning by developing a novel surface-to-image representation.

text: # Richard III Reburied in Leicester as Cumberbatch Reads Tribute Richard III, the King found beneath a car parking lot, has been reburied in a solemn but celebratory service, 530 years after his death in battle. The remains of the medieval monarch were sensationally rediscovered beneath a blanket of tarmac in the center of Leicester in August 2012. They have been pored over by scientists at the city's university ever since, but after more than two years of legal wranglings, the bones were finally laid to rest Thursday in a coffin built by Richard III's distant relative, Michael Ibsen, whose DNA helped prove their identity. It was standing room-only at Leicester Cathedral -- which had been partially rebuilt for the occasion -- as Archbishop of Canterbury Justin Welby led prayers for the long-dead King, swinging incense and sprinkling holy water over the casket, before scattering it with earth from key locations marking his birth, life and death. Oscar-nominated actor Benedict Cumberbatch, a distant cousin of England's last Plantagenet King, read a poem dedicated to Richard III, written by Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy. "My bones, scripted in light, upon cold soil, a human braille. My skull, scarred by a crown, emptied of history. Describe my soul as incense, votive, vanishing; your ownthe same. Five centuries after he fell at the Battle of Bosworth, King Richard III was finally laid to rest Thursday at Leicester Cathedral, in a service that blended medieval pageantry with modern celebrity. Grant me the carving of my name." Queen Elizabeth, represented at the ceremony by the Countess of Wessex, sent a special message to mark the reinterment, which she hailed as "an event of great national and international significance." "Today we recognize a King who lived through turbulent times and whose Christan faith sustained him in life and death," it read. The last Plantagenet king was killed in 1485 and buried hastily in the church of Leicester's Greyfriars friary.

text: The two-dimensional electron system formed at the interface between the insulating oxides LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 exhibits ferromagnetism, superconductivity, and a wide range of unique magnetotransport properties. A key challenge is to find a unified microscopic mechanism that underlies these emergent phenomena. The two-dimensional electron system that forms at the interface between the band insulators LaAlO₃ and SrTiO₃ displays a remarkable variety of behavior, including gate-tunable superconductivity, signatures of magnetism, strong spin–orbit coupling and unusual magnetotransport. Here we show that a universal Lifshitz transition between d-orbitals lies at the core of the observed transport phenomena in this system. Whether these phenomena share a common microscopic origin has remained an open question. Here we present systematic magnetotransport measurements, performed as a function of gate-controlled carrier density, on a series of interfaces with different LaAlO₃ thicknesses and electron mobilities. Our measurements find a critical electronic density at which the transport switches from single to multiple carriers. In every sample we identify a critical density of approximately 1.7 × 10¹³ cm⁻², at which transport changes abruptly from single-carrier to multi-carrier behavior.
